**Butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT)** is a food **antioxidant** ✓, added to fats, oils, butter,
biscuits and breakfast cereals to stop them going rancid.
Rancidity is an **oxidation**: atmospheric oxygen attacks the unsaturated fatty acids of a
fat by a **free-radical chain reaction**, producing short-chain aldehydes and acids with
unpleasant smells and tastes. BHT interrupts that chain.
Its structure explains how. BHT is a **phenol** with two bulky tert-butyl groups flanking the
–OH. It donates its phenolic hydrogen to a chain-carrying peroxide radical, quenching it; the
phenoxy radical left behind is **stabilised by the ring and shielded by the two bulky
groups**, so it is too unreactive to start a new chain. The chain is broken rather than
propagated.
Its close relative **BHA** (butylated hydroxyanisole) works the same way, and so does the
natural antioxidant **vitamin E**.
The other options name different classes of food additive:
**(b) flavouring agents** — esters, vanillin, and the like
**(c) colouring agents** — tartrazine, caramel
**(d) emulsifiers** — lecithin, which keeps oil and water mixed
All are additives, but only an antioxidant prevents the chemical spoilage that BHT is used
for.
∴ antioxidant.

Decide the class from what the **head group** carries.
**Stearic acid** (C₁₇H₃₅COOH) supplies the long hydrocarbon **tail**, and **polyethylene
glycol** supplies the head. They react to form an **ester**:
C₁₇H₃₅COOH + HO(CH₂CH₂O)ₙH ⟶ C₁₇H₃₅**COO**(CH₂CH₂O)ₙH + H₂O
The head is a long chain of **–OCH₂CH₂–** units ending in an –OH. It is water-soluble, but it
carries **no charge at all** — no sulphonate, no sulphate, no quaternary nitrogen. It
dissolves because of **hydrogen bonding** between its many ether oxygens and water.
A detergent whose head group is uncharged is a **non-ionic detergent** ✓ — option (d).
The three classes, for comparison:
**Anionic** — the head is negatively charged: sodium stearate (soap), sodium lauryl
sulphate, sodium dodecylbenzenesulphonate. Used in washing powders and toothpaste.
**Cationic** — the head is positively charged, usually a quaternary ammonium ion:
cetyltrimethylammonium bromide. Used in hair conditioners and as germicides.
**Non-ionic** — no charge: the polyethylene glycol esters. Used in liquid dishwashing
detergents.
Option (b), soap, would require a **sodium salt** of the acid rather than an ester, so the
ester linkage is what settles the answer.
∴ non-ionic detergent.

bacterial cell wall, so the wall fails and the cell bursts.

antibiotics. It is **bacteriostatic**: it resembles *p*-aminobenzoic acid closely enough to

is what makes an antibacterial usable as a medicine.

it covers antibiotics (made by living organisms), sulpha drugs and wholly synthetic agents

pradeep|Chemistry|0|64|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Take the two statements separately.
**Statement-1: 'Ranitidine is used to treat hyperacidity while brompheniramine is used to
treat hypersensitivity.'** ✓ **True.**
**Ranitidine** (Zantac) suppresses the secretion of stomach acid and is the standard
treatment for hyperacidity and ulcers.
**Brompheniramine** (Dimetane) relieves the sneezing, itching and congestion of allergy —
that is, hypersensitivity.
**Statement-2: 'Both the drugs are antihistamines.'** ✓ **True**, and this is the part that
looks wrong at first sight.
Both drugs act by **blocking histamine receptors**; they differ only in **which** receptor:
**Ranitidine** blocks **H₂** receptors, found on the parietal cells of the **stomach**. With
histamine shut out, acid is not secreted.
**Brompheniramine** blocks **H₁** receptors, found in the skin, airways and blood vessels.
With histamine shut out there, the allergic response is suppressed.
So both statements are true, and statement-2 correctly explains statement-1: the same class
of drug produces two quite different therapeutic effects because histamine has two kinds of
receptor doing two different jobs. Recognising that there were two kinds was the insight
that made ranitidine and cimetidine possible.
∴ both statement-1 and statement-2 are true.

Note: the printed key gives (b), both false. Statement-1 states the two drugs' uses
correctly, and statement-2 is correct because ranitidine is an H₂-antihistamine and
brompheniramine an H₁-antihistamine, so the key is wrong and has been corrected to (a).
